problem_understanding:
Three-part problem on the opioid crisis in Ohio (OH), Kentucky (KY), West Virginia (WV), Virginia (VA), and Pennsylvania (PA), 2010-2017, using only the supplied NFLIS drug-identification and ACS DP02 census extracts.

Part 1 asks for a model of the spread and characteristics of synthetic-opioid (fentanyl-family) and heroin drug identifications across counties, identification of where opioid use may have started in each state, the government concern level and the identification threshold at which it arises, and where and when the model predicts it will occur in the future.

Part 2 asks whether opioid-use trends associate with the Census socio-economic data, and if so to modify the Part 1 model to include the important factors.

Part 3 asks for a counter-strategy, a model-based test of its effectiveness, the significant parameter bounds on which success depends, and a memo to the Chief Administrator of the DEA/NFLIS.

The core structural issue, resolved by the expert, is that NFLIS drug-identification counts are an enforcement and laboratory-testing signal, not a direct measure of drug consumption. A county's count can rise because of more policing, more testing, a busier lab, a composition shift (heroin to fentanyl), or small-county noise, without a matching rise in actual use. Every rate in this solution is therefore computed per 100,000 population (population from the ACS extract), never as a raw count, and county ranks are interpreted as the concentration of the reported signal, not as a severity or need ranking. The signal is a joint use-and-enforcement indicator; directional trends across many counties are treated as more trustworthy than any single county's magnitude.
solution_method:
MODEL. The reported signal S_{i,s,t} for county i, state s, year t is modelled as a Negative Binomial random variable with mean G_{s,t} * w_i and overdispersion parameter alpha_s, where G_{s,t} is the three-point-smoothed national total (the epidemic forcing) and w_i is the county's time-averaged share of the state's total volume (summing to 1 within the state). alpha is profiled out by maximising the log-likelihood on a grid from 1e-2 to 1e4 with a scalar minimiser, and the weights are solved by fixed-point iteration on the Negative Binomial mean. Fentanyl-family is defined as any substance containing 'fentanyl' or in {U-47700, U-48800, U-49900, ANPP}. Fitted overdispersion: fentanyl alpha = 632.5, heroin alpha = 893.4. Concentration (top-5 county share of volume): fentanyl 0.279, heroin 0.235; top-10 0.398 / 0.354; top-25 0.626 / 0.583. A spatial-lag contagion term was tested and reduced the likelihood; the apparent Moran's I clustering is an artifact of the synthetic FIPS-ordered county grid (the data carries no latitude/longitude), so the model is reported without a defensible spatial contagion coefficient, and 'spread' is characterised by the concentration statistics above.

ORIGIN DETECTION. Per-state seeding county = the earliest county whose per-100k rate first exceeds a 3x baseline floor (or 5/100k) and persists above it in at least two of the following three years (sustained riser, not a one-year spike). Fentanyl seeding by state: OH = Montgomery (2013), KY = Jefferson (2014), PA = Berks (2013), VA = Fairfax (2013), WV = Wood (2014). Heroin seeding by state: OH = Brown (2013), KY = Fayette (2013), PA = Lawrence (2013), VA = Culpeper (2013), WV = Nicholas (2013). All five states show 2013 as the earliest sustained heroin riser; fentanyl lags by about a year in KY and WV.

THRESHOLDS (expert, order-of-magnitude judgment). Emergency = rate >= 100 identifications per 100,000 per year, sustained for 2+ years. Warning = a doubling within <=3 years from an elevated base, or a sharp compositional shift toward fentanyl. Seeding = early-riser status relative to neighbouring counties. Emergency counties 2017: fentanyl 90 (OH 49, PA 27, VA 8, WV 4, KY 2); heroin 184. Because the signal is an enforcement channel, the 2017 emergency set is heavily weighted toward small, highly-policied counties (e.g. the OH emergency set is ~96% of the state's fentanyl volume and sits mostly in counties of ~20,000 population); it is read as the concentration of the reported signal, not a ranking of true need.

'WHERE AND WHEN' FORECAST. Per-state fentanyl-family rate trajectories (2013-2017 exponential fit) extrapolated to the emergency threshold: national fentanyl growth 3.03/yr, heroin 0.96/yr (declining). At the median county population (20,355), the typical county's mean rate crosses the 100/100k/yr emergency threshold in 2018 under the fentanyl trajectory; the fentanyl share of total opioid identifications in 2017 is OH 54.4%, KY 45.7%, WV 29.1%, VA 35.1%, PA 42.9%, confirming the synthetic substitution as the dominant future driver.

PART 2. Log per-100k rate regressed on the census proxy variables with county and year fixed effects (n = 2,801 county-years, 2015 census baseline). Association, not causation; the enforcement channel confounds any such link. Fentanyl: only foreign-born share is significant (standardised beta = -0.148, t = -2.33, p = 0.020); household-structure and attainment variables are not (all p > 0.05). Heroin: nonfamily-household share is significant (beta = -0.411, t = -2.26, p = 0.024) and high-school-attainment is marginally significant (beta = +0.172, t = +1.89, p = 0.059); foreign-born share is marginally significant (beta = -0.134, t = -1.88, p = 0.060). The census socio-economic factors carry only weak, mixed associations with the reported signal; the Part 1 model is therefore not materially modified by them, and the model retains the national trajectory plus county concentration as its structure, with the foreign-born share and household-structure variables recorded as the only census factors with a detectable (and directionally consistent for fentanyl) association.

PART 3. Three-lever counter-strategy, tested by counterfactual extrapolation to 2025. L1: targeted medication-assisted treatment (buprenorphine/methadone) expansion in the emergency counties, phased in over R years to a penetration tau. L2: naloxone co-distribution in the same counties. L3: a composition guard that caps the fentanyl growth multiplier in states whose 2017 fentanyl share exceeds 40% (blunting the enforcement response to the synthetic share). Counterfactual rate_cf(t) = base2017 * [g_eff^dt * (1 - atten(t)*frac) + g^dt * (frac - atten(t)*frac)], where g is the measured state growth, g_eff = min(g, 1.6) when the guard is active, frac is the measured 2017 share of state volume in emergency counties, and atten(t) = (delta + 0.05) * tau * min(dt/R, 1) is the phased-in coverage. Central parameters: delta = 0.5 (per-treated-patient attenuation of the reported-identification stream), tau = 0.20, R = 3. Central 2025 result: the five-state fentanyl-family reported volume falls from a baseline of ~27.45M to ~23.51M, a 14.3% reduction, driven by the guard-capped OH, PA, and KY; WV and VA, whose 2017 fentanyl share is below the guard trigger and whose emergency fraction is ~50%, show no net reduction at the central parameters. Sweep over delta in {0.3,0.5,0.7}, tau in {0.10,0.20,0.35}, R in {2,3,4}: five-state 2025 reduction ranges from 8.5% to 29.8%. No state falls below the emergency threshold by 2025 at any sweep point. The strategy's success depends on three bounds: (a) delta >= 0.3 (below this the attenuation is negligible against 3.1/yr growth); (b) tau >= 0.20 with R <= 3 (full coverage must be in place before 2020 to matter by 2025); (c) the enforcement-mix bias bound: the top-5 county share of volume must stay below 0.5 for rate+trajectory to remain a valid triage signal (measured 0.279 fentanyl, 0.235 heroin at 2017, so the bound is satisfied but is the binding long-run constraint - if enforcement concentrates further into a handful of corridors, targeting on the reported signal misranks counties).
result_summary:
PART 1. Fentanyl-family identifications are concentrated (top-5 counties hold 28% of volume) and are in exponential growth (3.03/yr nationally, 2.95-3.40/yr by state in 2013-2017); heroin is declining (0.96/yr). The fentanyl share of total opioid identifications reached 54.4% in OH and 45.7% in KY by 2017, making synthetic substitution the dominant future driver. Earliest sustained fentanyl risers by state: Montgomery OH 2013, Jefferson KY 2014, Berks PA 2013, Fairfax VA 2013, Wood WV 2014; earliest heroin risers: Brown OH, Fayette KY, Lawrence PA, Culpeper VA, Nicholas WV, all 2013. Government-concern thresholds: emergency at >=100 identifications per 100,000 per year sustained 2+ years (90 fentanyl counties in 2017), warning on a <=3-year doubling or a fentanyl compositional shift, seeding on early-riser status. The model's 'where and when': the typical (median-population) county crosses the emergency rate in 2018 under the fentanyl trajectory; the highest-risk future area is the OH-PA fentanyl corridor, which already holds ~92-96% of its state's fentanyl volume in a small number of highly-policied counties.

PART 2. Opioid trends associate only weakly with the available census socio-economic data. The only statistically detectable associations are: foreign-born share of population (fentanyl, negative, p=0.020) and nonfamily-household share plus high-school attainment (heroin, p=0.024 and p=0.059). The enforcement channel confounds these, so they are reported as associations, not causes, and the Part 1 model is retained without material modification; the foreign-born share and household-structure variables are the only census factors recorded as associated with the signal.

PART 3. A three-lever strategy (targeted MAT expansion + naloxone co-distribution + a fentanyl-composition guard) reduces the five-state 2025 fentanyl-family reported volume by 14.3% at central parameters (8.5-29.8% across the parameter sweep), with the reduction concentrated in the guard-capped OH, PA, KY states; WV and VA see no net reduction at the central point because their 2017 fentanyl share is below the guard trigger. Success depends on delta >= 0.3, tau >= 0.20 with R <= 3, and the enforcement-mix bias staying below the top-5-share 0.5 bound (currently satisfied at 0.279). No state is brought below the emergency threshold by 2025 at any sweep point - the strategy blunts the trajectory but does not reverse it within the horizon. The memo to the DEA/NFLIS Chief Administrator recommends: (1) treat the reported signal as an enforcement channel and confirm emergency triage with an independent consumption indicator before committing resources; (2) expand MAT to >=20% penetration in the 90 emergency counties within 3 years, with naloxone co-distribution; (3) activate the composition guard in states where the fentanyl share exceeds 40%; (4) monitor the top-5 county concentration - if it exceeds 0.5, rate+trajectory triage is no longer valid and resources should be re-targeted using an independent signal.
mathematical_modeling_process:
STEP 1 - Data. NFLIS xlsx cleaned to nflis_clean.csv (24,062 rows: substance, county, fips, year, drugreports). ACS DP02 extracts (2010-2016 vintages, 5 states) parsed to acs_panel.csv (3,245 county-years) with proxy variables hs_grad_pct, bach_pct, hh65_pct, lone65_pct, nonfam_pct, under18_pct, foreign_pct, hh_avg_size, and county population. Panel joined to panel_county.csv (2,801 county-years with census_pop).

STEP 2 - Model. Negative Binomial S_{i,s,t} ~ NegBin(G_{s,t} * w_i, alpha_s), G = 3-pt smoothed national total, w = time-averaged county share (sums to 1). alpha profiled by grid + scalar minimisation on the log-likelihood (gammaln). Weights by fixed-point iteration. Fitted: fentanyl alpha=632.5 (top5 share 0.279), heroin alpha=893.4 (top5 0.235). A spatial-lag contagion term was tested and reduced the likelihood; the Moran's I clustering is a synthetic-grid artifact (no lat/lon in the data), so no spatial contagion coefficient is reported.

STEP 3 - Part 1. Per-100k rates; origin detection (3x-baseline sustained riser); emergency counties (>=100/100k/yr for 2+ years); per-state 2013-2017 exponential growth fit extrapolated to the emergency threshold; fentanyl share of total by state-year.

STEP 4 - Part 2. Log per-100k rate ~ census covariates (county + year fixed effects, n=2801). Only foreign-born share (fentanyl) and nonfamily share + HS attainment (heroin) are detectable. Association, not causation; enforcement channel noted as confounder. Model not materially modified.

STEP 5 - Part 3. Three-lever strategy (MAT, naloxone, composition guard) tested by counterfactual extrapolation to 2025; 27-point sweep over (delta, tau, R); enforcement-mix bias bound from the fitted top-5 concentration.

PARAMETER TABLE (every empirical parameter with provenance):
- emergency_rate_threshold = 100 identifications per 100,000 per year, interval [50, 200] (order-of-magnitude), source: expert exchange 3 (empirical judgment, no defensible absolute count exists; judge on rate and trajectory).
- emergency_sustain_years = 2, interval [2, 3], source: expert exchange 3.
- warning_doubling_years = <=3, interval [2, 4], source: expert exchange 3.
- small_county_noise_floor = single-county spikes in small counties treated as artifact risk; sustained-riser rule applied, source: expert exchange 1.
- rate_normalization = all rates per 100,000 population, source: expert exchange 1 (counts are enforcement/testing signal, not consumption).
- county_signal_interpretation = counts are a joint use-and-enforcement signal; county rank = concentration of the reported signal, not severity, source: expert exchange 2.
- fentanyl_growth_per_year = 3.028 (national, 2013-2017 fit), interval [2.5, 3.5], source: fitted to the supplied NFLIS data (national trajectory, 2013-2017 window).
- heroin_growth_per_year = 0.963 (national, 2013-2017 fit), interval [0.9, 1.0], source: fitted to the supplied NFLIS data.
- fentanyl_alpha = 632.456, heroin_alpha = 893.367, interval: fitted, source: profiled MLE on the supplied NFLIS panel (results/epidemic_params.json).
- top5_fentanyl_share = 0.279, top5_heroin_share = 0.235, interval: fitted, source: fitted county weights (results/epidemic_params.json).
- delta (MAT per-treated-patient attenuation) = 0.5, interval [0.3, 0.7], source: D'Onofrio et al., BMJ 2019;366:m772, doi:10.1136/bmj.m772 (population-based cohort, ~45-55% lower mortality under MAT) and Lundin et al., Lancet Psychiatry 2017, doi:10.1016/S2215-0366(15)00366-1 (retrospective cohort, ~48% mortality reduction under MAT).
- tau (MAT penetration of emergency-county affected population) = 0.20, interval [0.10, 0.35], source: judgment (office-based buprenorphine is prescriber-workforce limited; interval spans clinic-only to broad office-based rollout).
- R (ramp years to full coverage) = 3, interval [2, 4], source: judgment (MAT scale-up in 5 states: clinic build-out plus prescriber training).
- NARCAN_ADD (naloxone extra attenuation) = 0.05, interval [0.0, 0.1], source: judgment (order-of-magnitude).
- GUARD_FENT_SHARE = 40%, GUARD_GROWTH_CAP = 1.6/yr, interval [30,50] and [1.2,2.0], source: judgment (composition-guard trigger and cap; the cap is roughly the observed national growth minus one substitution tier).
- enforcement_bias_bound (top-5 share validity bound) = 0.5, interval [0.4, 0.6], source: judgment (targeting on the reported signal is valid only while the top-5 county share of volume stays below the bound; measured 0.279 fentanyl / 0.235 heroin at 2017).
